title: Qrita: High-performance Top-k and Top-p Algorithm for GPUs using Pivot-based Truncation and Selection
claim: Pivot search with percentile and softmax-CDF thresholds finds the selection cutoff in a few iterations without sorting.
layout: Top: 21-line pseudocode with comments; bottom: two side-by-side density plots
description: The figure has two parts separated by a horizontal rule. The top is a numbered 21-line algorithm listing for quaternary pivot search. It has bold keywords (Input, Output, while, for, if, return), math notation (tau pivots, l and r bounds, counts N, duplicate handling), and right-aligned // comments explaining each step. The bottom has two small plots of a standard-normal logit density over the logit value z from -4 to 4. The left plot, 'Percentile (Top-k)', has a blue curve, a dark-red dashed cutoff line labeled delta_k, a red-shaded right tail, and a k/vocab_size annotation with an arrow. The right plot, 'Softmax CDF (Top-p)', has a dotted blue density, a green rising softmax-probability curve, an orange dashed cutoff delta_p, an orange-shaded tail, and a p label. The eye goes first to the dense pseudocode, then to the colored plots.
caption: Gaussian σ-truncation on logits following a standard normal distribution.
abstract: Despite their importance in model sampling, efficient implementation of the Top-k and Top-p algorithms poses a significant challenge as model vocabulary grows with each new model release. Existing approaches often rely on sorting, which incurs significant computation and memory overhead on GPUs, or on stochastic approaches that alter the algorithm's output. In this work, we propose Qrita, an efficient Top-k and Top-p algorithm based on pivot-based truncation and selection. Qrita leverages pivot-based search for both Top-k and Top-p with two key techniques: 1. Gaussian-based sigma-truncation, which limits the complexity of the algorithm to O(n), and 2. Quaternary pivot search with duplication handling, which halves the number of pivot search iterations and guarantees deterministic output. We implement Qrita using Triton and evaluate its performance against the Top-k and Top-p kernels of high-performance LLM execution engines such as SGLang and FlashInfer, improving end-to-end serving throughput up to 1.4 times with half the memory usage, while providing the same output as stable sort-based Top-k and Top-p algorithms. Qrita is now the default Triton Top-k and Top-p sampler of vLLM, and its implementation is available at https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/sample/ops/topk_topp_triton.py.
